items.title: GitHub availability report: September 2026
items.summary: In September, we experienced two incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services. The post GitHub availability report: September 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months.

The short version of August and September : we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete.

By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added.

We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. We disabled that process during planned handoffs while improving recovery.

Outside the regional migration, 24 authentication-core tables moved off GitHub’s oldest shared database, removing approximately one million queries per second from its replicas. The database cluster supporting issues and pull requests removed approximately 980 million unnecessary edit-history rows, creating an estimated 1.8 terabytes of recoverable storage. Weekly deadlocks fell approximately 77% from their June peak, and continuous cleanup now prevents the same unbounded growth from returning.

Half of sampled pull request traffic can now continue with limited functionality when a shared dependency fails. Production results showed several read operations remained available during a shared-database incident. Database traffic routing can also add capacity automatically during spikes; one group expanded from 14 to 19 instances during a September 23 increase in pull request activity. A production overload control now lets responders protect higher-priority API and web workflows by rejecting lower-priority requests before broader saturation. Operator documentation and training are complete.

GitHub Actions also gained operating headroom. Production changes reduced measured Redis operations by approximately 28% and relative CPU by approximately 30%. A separate infrastructure cache reduced Redis bandwidth by 84%, average response time by 66%, median response time for the primary inventory request by 96%, and queued requests by 95%.

The August 6 actions outage, August 17 github.com outage, September failover disruption, and controlled capacity pause are reminders that measured improvements matter only when they reduce customer risk under real conditions. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

A background data-cleanup job increased load on a shared database. The job had a safeguard designed to slow its writes when database replicas fell behind, but the safeguard did not account for incoming load on the primary database server. As a result, the job continued running until the primary reached its connections limit. When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that depended on it could not complete reliably.

Two other factors increased the impact and delayed recovery. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept resending writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover.

Copilot code review uses a separate service to run reviews and 2 versions of the results are returned: a limited copy that excludes the review comments and a full copy that includes the completed review. Copilot code review posts reviews only from the full copy. A change to that service began sending the full copy only for some customers. For other customers, only the limited copy was sent.

As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully. The missing review results were not detected due to lack of monitoring. The incident was detected as some of the reviews remained incomplete for more than 30 minutes, triggering an alert to first responders.

We mitigated the incident by reverting the change.

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog .

items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
items.summary: Our new repo star history API now provides trends without returning individual identities or requiring unbounded database work. These are the engineering tradeoffs we made. The post From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers appeared first on The Gi
items.content:
Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away.

Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page.

The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper.

Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything .

We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators . After the access change, callers without the required permission could receive an empty response or a 403 Forbidden response.

That change also cut off tools that had used the old response to calculate star history, often without displaying or otherwise using the usernames it returned. So we talked with maintainers and tool builders to understand what they still needed. They used star history as an approximate signal of interest: to compare activity before and after a release, or to see whether an announcement reached new developers. What they cared about was the curve.

The old API response had made identity look like part of that contract because every timestamp arrived attached to a user. In practice, tools such as Star History needed counts and dates, not usernames or other user data. Once identity was no longer part of the requirement, we could design an aggregate endpoint for the actual job: retrieving changes in star counts over time at a useful resolution.

When the API change disrupted Star History, users rallied around the project. GitHub’s Community team listened and connected us with product engineering, who dug into our use case and worked alongside us to design a purpose-built endpoint. A difficult situation became a constructive collaboration between GitHub, Star History, and the broader community—ultimately leading to a better solution.

Once we knew what maintainers needed, the next step was understanding why the original design couldn’t provide it cheaply. The original GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers endpoint was built to answer a simple question: who starred this repository? It returned a paginated list of people, and if the request specified a custom media type, each entry also included when the star was created.

The star model was built for the same job. It records the current set of people who have starred a repository, which keeps showing a star count or a list of stargazers simple. It was not designed as a historical event log: when someone removes a star, that record is removed. When tools began using the list as a time series, reconstructing a growth curve meant retrieving individual identities and processing every current star. Because each page held at most 100 people, the work grew with the repository’s popularity: building the full curve for react/react , with about 251,000 stars, took about 2,511 requests, so tools often ran into rate limits or sampled pages instead of reading them all.

Serving a page required the database to query the repository’s current stars. Due to a bug in the pagination implementation, every request also counted all of those stars to work out how many pages existed, even though the caller received only one page of up to 100 people. On a highly starred repository, that meant counting many thousands of entries on every request. In the week before we restricted access, nearly 37,000 of these count queries ran slowly enough to be logged, averaging nearly 3 seconds each, and database safeguards killed more than 1,000 of them, which contributed to request timeouts.

The chart below shows what all that counting cost. After we restricted access, the database served about 60% fewer stargazer requests, and the total time it spent on the count query fell by about 80%.

Removing identities handled the privacy requirement. The harder part was keeping each request from scanning the repository’s entire current star set.

Our first spike kept one record per star and returned the starred_at value without the stargazer’s identity for callers who lacked collaborator access. At first, this looked like the quickest path forward, because it directly served the request we had heard from tool builders. It also closed the identity-harvesting path with a relatively small change to the existing serialization and authorization flow.

This approach addressed identity exposure and would have allowed existing tools to keep working. But API consumers would still have to paginate through and process potentially many thousands of individual records to build an aggregate history. It also tied the new use case to an endpoint and pagination model designed for listing people rather than retrieving trends.

Aggregation seemed like the obvious next step. Instead of returning one row per star, the query could group stars into daily or weekly buckets, sort those buckets, and paginate the much smaller result.

items.title: The AI race is back on
items.summary: Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions, h
items.content:
Google and Meta are challenging Anthropic and OpenAI at the AI frontier.﻿

Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions , had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China , impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up.

Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic. Suddenly, the race is back on — and it’s anyone’s game.

Until this week, Google looked like it had permanently lost its place among the AI front-runners. Since releasing Gemini 3 late last year, the tech giant had delivered little more than incremental improvements. Gemini 3 was formidable when it launched, but its lead was fleeting, and it struggled to keep up with later offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, or even some of the open-weight models emerging from China.

A series of internal shake-ups only added to the sense that Google was retreating from the AI frontier. Veteran executive Jeff Dean departed the company with a number of other AI researchers to launch a new startup. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who spent years at the helm of Google’s AI powerhouse DeepMind, stepped back from day-to-day leadership. Other AI-related teams were moved out of DeepMind and into Google proper. Together, the changes signaled a broader shift in Google’s AI center of gravity, moving away from London and toward California, fueling speculation the tech giant was beginning to prioritize commercializing AI over research.

Then, on Tuesday, Google upended that narrative with the release of Gemini 4 Argon , a new frontier model the company claims matches or beats flagship offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic on numerous benchmarks, whatever value benchmarks are still worth. What’s more, Google has priced Argon aggressively: Per token, it’s undercutting its rivals by as much as 80 percent during its introductory period, and is still significantly cheaper once that promotion ends.

Meta’s arrival was arguably even more dramatic. Unlike Google, which had long been the one to beat in AI thanks to its deep pockets and DeepMind, Meta had never really established itself as a serious contender at the frontier. It was not through lack of trying, but its models struggled to make a mark. Last year, the company embarked on an ambitious and expensive overhaul of its AI operations, spending billions on talent and infrastructure, including Scale AI and its cofounder Alexandr Wang. In April, its new Superintelligence Labs released its first major model, Muse Spark. Impressive, but not quite frontier.

That changed on Monday when Meta finally unveiled a model capable of competing with the industry’s very best. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder Full can compete with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, on numerous benchmarks. In other words, Mark Zuckerberg’s company has finally arrived at the AI frontier.

The return of Google — and the arrival of Meta — makes the AI competition considerably more dynamic and shows just how quickly the balance of power can shift in the AI world. Both have extraordinarily deep pockets and vast ecosystems of products used by billions of people, advantages that AI upstarts like OpenAI and Anthropic simply cannot match. The success of Meta’s Muse agent assistant illustrates that advantage. Its popularity in such a short period of time, and despite the growing list of security and privacy concerns, shows the power of having billions of users within ready reach. OpenAI, meanwhile, is having to work harder to establish an ecosystem of its own, positioning itself as an alternative to Meta.

All this comes as the AI race appears to be entering a new phase. The drive to develop ever more powerful models is becoming increasingly fraught. The growing array of safety concerns and rogue AI incidents means calls to slow development are growing louder. Open models are also getting better and better, making it harder for any one company to stay ahead for long.

If raw power and performance are no longer enough to stay ahead, Google and Meta have plenty of advantages not enjoyed by Anthropic and OpenAI. They may have spent a lot of time playing catch-up, but the past week shows it would be incredibly foolish to count either of them out.

items.title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2026/10/13/suicide-rates-highest-ever-among-middle-aged-men/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50093180 Points: 353 # Comments: 444
items.content:
Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed.

Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics .

There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly.

Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”.

He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.”

The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health ”.

Mr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.”

The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people.

The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population.

Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981.

For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk.

Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024.

Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”.

She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.”

The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44.

There were 19.5 deaths per 100,000 men aged 25 to 44 last year, which is the widest gap since 2009, when middle-aged male suicide rates overtook those of younger adults. The rate increased from 14 to 14.4 per 100,000 for those aged 65 to 74 and from 13.2 to 15.4 among those aged 75 or older.

Marjorie Wallace, the chief executive of mental health charity Sane, said she was “not surprised” by the data. She said: “Analysis of the contact we receive reflects this – almost 60 per cent of our callers now talk about suicide or self-harm, a very different picture than 10 years ago.

“While middle-aged men in their forties and fifties still remain at greatest risk, our other concern is the number of young people, particularly girls and women aged 16 to 24, who report anxiety and depression on a scale not experienced before.”

items.title: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?
items.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding. James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Charact
items.content:
State AGs are now trying to make sure its users’ private chats aren’t exposed to the highest bidder.﻿

New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation against Character.AI as they now seek to require protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy proceeding.

James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in Character.AI’s bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.” Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney. But the AGs warn there could be serious risk involved in the transfer of the technology due to the “highly sensitive nature of the conversations many users have with Character.AI chatbot characters, the large number of minors who use the product, the serious risks posed by specific features of the product.”

The filing also reveals that several of the states had been mid-investigation when Character.AI filed for bankruptcy. The states say they opened a probe into consumer protection and privacy concerns in 2024, following a lawsuit from the mother of a 14-year-old who died by suicide allegedly “seconds” after talking with the chatbot.

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers”

“The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws,” according to a press release from James’ office. The states were working to address these issues with Character.AI, but didn’t reach an agreement before the company filed for bankruptcy. Character.AI and Disney did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The states are urging the judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement procedures that will safeguard the sensitive information the company maintained. Those include effective age-assurance systems, restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots, implementing “Crisis safeguards,” and letting users delete their data. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said in a statement. “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

items.title: As a TV enthusiast, I was hoping for more from the Apple TV 4K
items.summary: It's been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration - the 2022 Apple TV
items.content:
The new Apple TV 4K streaming box has a very premium price tag and doesn’t add desired home theater features.

Photography by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

It’s been four long years since the last Apple TV 4K was released, and in that time there have been lots of hopes and dreams for features in whatever comes next. A new chip, 4K/120Hz support, audio passthrough, a remote locator, better home control integration — the 2022 Apple TV 4K is a great box, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement. With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K announced on Tuesday, some of those hopes were met, while others were unfortunately left out.

Coloring the announcement is the device’s price. Apple eliminated the cheaper 64GB, Wi-Fi-only model, leaving just the 128GB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet model — and bumped up its price to $300. I repeat, $300 for a streaming device. It’s a hefty price when every other major streamer on the market is at least half the cost.

There are new features I like about this year’s Apple TV 4K. More processing power is great — although my third generation is still running plenty fast — as is the Find My support for when the remote inevitably gets lost in the couch cushions or tangled up in blankets. Built-in far-field mics for talking to Siri are nice, too, provided you don’t stuff the box into a credenza like I do. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K also adds a dedicated AV1 decoder, which allows for higher-quality streaming from apps that support it, such as Netflix, which is excellent. Any potential improvement to streaming content is a welcome one.

My primary concern, though, is how the Apple TV 4K performs as an integral piece of my home theater. Apple added the ability to create a surround sound system by using its HomePod 2 and HomePod Mini 2 smart speakers in matching pairs for fronts and surrounds. For Apple ecosystem fans looking to build out a surround setup akin to Sonos or Bose, it’s an interesting idea (and I’m all for getting people into immersive sound in their home theaters). But as I expect is the same for many people interested in pricey streaming hardware, I already have a sound system — it’s an Atmos setup with a combination of SVS and Revel speakers. I’m not setting up my two HomePod 2s in my living room and spending another $300 on a pair of HomePod Mini 2s to replace my existing speakers.

What I, and many current users, have been hoping for from the Apple TV 4K for years is the addition of audio passthrough. This would allow my more expensive and capable audio/video receiver to decode the raw audio stream instead of the Apple TV using its Continuous Audio Connection, which can cause some playback issues .

Additionally, it would have been nice to see Apple support 120fps output, especially for those who use Moonlight to stream games to it . That’s a feature that would have set the Apple TV 4K apart from all the other streamers, which top out at 60fps, and helped to justify the high price. Apple could have also used it to pivot more into TV gaming. (For movies, though, the 60fps limit is not a huge deal, as the box can be set to output 24fps, allowing a native 120Hz TV to just use 5:5 pulldown.)

Other premium features that would set Apple’s streaming box apart and make home theater enthusiasts throw their money at it include an HDMI input for HDMI passthrough or a digital optical out. I understand leaving them out if it meant raising the price further. This box is already expensive enough. But it does leave the Apple TV 4K in an uncomfortable spot, pairing a high-end price with features that are largely matched elsewhere for much less.

Are these high-end omissions a concern for the majority of people? Not really. But those people are going to look at the $300 price tag of the Apple TV 4K and then at Google, Roku, or Amazon streaming devices, which are all half that price or less. The Apple TV 4K is looked at as the premium streamer option, but the now extra premium price without some of the, admittedly niche, features gives me pause.

Maybe the new Apple TV 4K will surprise me. I’ve certainly been looking forward to it for a while . I already appreciate the way Apple handles privacy, and if Apple adds features in coming months, maybe it could be worth it. But that $300 price? It might be better spent elsewhere in your home theater setup.

items.summary: Article URL: https://dpa-international.com/politics/urn:newsml:dpa.com:20090101:261014-930-839530/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50092730 Points: 321 # Comments: 209
items.content:
14.10.2026, 20:51 Uhr

By Elena Lalowa, dpa

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Wednesday that there had been a fire at a facility of the Starlink satellite internet service near the capital Sofia last week.

Two young men holding German passports have been taken into custody in connection with the suspected attack, Bulgarian media later reported, citing investigators.

The satellite network is a strategically important part of Ukraine's defence in the war against Russia's invasion.

The fire had previously been made public by the pro-Western opposition alliance Democratic Bulgaria (DB). Radev said he would not provide any further details in light of the ongoing investigations.

According to DB, 11 of 17 antennas at a Starlink facility near Sofia were deliberately set on fire on October 9. The antennas were used in the war in Ukraine, DB said.

Pro-Western opposition parties said they suspected Russia was linked to the attack.

Two men aged 20 and 21, both holding German passports, were detained in Bulgaria on Monday in connection with the suspected attack, several Bulgarian media outlets reported on Wednesday evening, citing investigators.

According to the news outlet Faktor.bg, the two suspects have migrant backgrounds and had legally entered Bulgaria from Greece through the Kulata border crossing.

The website reported that investigators were examining whether the suspects belonged to a larger sabotage network potentially linked to two men arrested in Germany earlier this week over a recent attack on a Starlink facility in Poland.

Bulgarian officials stressed that the Starlink facility near Sofia was privately owned.

Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told parliament that additional security measures had been introduced at similar facilities, even though responsibility for their protection rested with their owners.

Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria's State Agency for National Security (DANS), said he believed the fire at the Starlink facility was an act of sabotage.

"Such acts of sabotage cannot be ruled out in the future either," he warned lawmakers.

A fire also broke out at a Starlink ground terminal south of Warsaw on September 23.

Two suspected saboteurs accused of carrying out that attack in Poland were arrested on Tuesday in Nürtingen, near Stuttgart in south-western Germany.

The government in Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence services were behind the attack.

items.title: YouTube sticks new labels on AI-generated songs
items.summary: YouTube is adding a "Made with AI" label to tracks that were "altered or fully generated" using AI, with a similar approach to its existing process for applying AI labels to videos. It doesn't sound like this will apply to any and all use of AI tools in making music, but accordin
items.content:
New AI labels are marking tracks created ‘primarily’ with generative AI tools, starting first on YouTube Music.

YouTube is adding a “Made with AI” label to tracks that were “altered or fully generated” using AI, with a similar approach to its existing process for applying AI labels to videos . It doesn’t sound like this will apply to any and all use of AI tools in making music, but according to YouTube, it includes things like “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” In its rules for music partners who upload their songs, YouTube lays out how to disclose generative AI use, and says that if there’s no disclosure, it may use “other signals” to decide if a song is AI-generated.

The label is rolling out starting today in the YouTube Music app, and expanding to the main YouTube app later.

You’ll be able to see more details by tapping the label on the player page:

When you listen to a track on YouTube Music where AI played a significant role, you’ll see a label directly on the player page. Tapping the label opens a simple menu that shares more information.

We’re teaming up with music partners and using our own detection tools to identify AI-generated tracks, applying the same labeling principles already used across YouTube. Our goal is to make it as easy as possible for viewers and listeners to have the right information and clarity when it comes to the music they listen to.

Spotify launched a voluntary AI label earlier this year and said that it wouldn’t recommend songs from “AI personas,” and Apple Music is also reportedly getting an AI tag . Other music platforms are taking things even further to push back against AI-generated music — Deezer added a switch for filtering out AI tracks , and Bandcamp banned AI music outright earlier this year.

items.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
items.summary: AI may soon be the default way to solve theoretical problems in economics, high-energy physics, and other fields, MIT researchers tell WIRED.
items.content:
Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence . Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.

As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.

“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.

Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun , a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.

Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.

The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.

Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes , which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.

OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI , warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.

As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.

Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science , and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.

“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”

items.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.csoonline.com/article/4234854/ai-agents-arent-going-rogue-frontier-labs-are-skipping-security-basics.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50091788 Points: 854 # Comments: 491
items.content:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

[ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ]

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

items.content:
Apple’s first smart display doesn’t arrive until November 13th, but you can save on a couple of colorways.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Apple only just announced on Tuesday that its first smart display, the HomeView , will arrive on November 13th, but you can already save a couple bucks on it. Right now, you can buy the display for $289.99 ($10 off) in gray and the creamy white “starlight” colorway at Amazon. Sure, it’s a small discount, but deals on new Apple devices ahead of launch are rare.

Expect a full review of the HomeView in November, but my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy spent some brief time with it and likened it to an “iPhone for your home” that looks a bit like an oversized Apple Watch. It features a gorgeous seven-inch square touchscreen that can recognize up to six household members and automatically switch between personalized experiences, displaying information relevant to whoever is using it.

As you might already know, the HomeView also doubles as a smart home hub, with support for Matter and Thread. You can use it to control compatible smart home devices, view live feeds and recorded footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and more. It also features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera for video calls, and doubles as an entertainment device, letting you play music, display photos, and more.

Apple’s AI-powered Siri assistant is another big part of the experience, allowing you to ask questions and get information using personal context from your messages, calendar, and emails. That means you can ask it to find your lost keys, play a song someone texted you, pull up a recipe with step-by-step instructions and built-in timers, or help you keep track of your schedule without having to reach for your phone.

items.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
items.summary: AI design tools make proteins that break bonds that are stable for hundreds of years.
items.content:
A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they’re estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth’s environment, most proteins don’t last nearly that long. That’s because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment.

Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases.

The basic peptide bond isn’t especially interesting-looking—it’s what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.)

Breaking these bonds apart simply reverses the process by breaking apart the peptide bond and a water molecule, and linking their parts. Because both components are chemically stable, the reaction requires an enzyme to occur with any frequency. Without an enzyme, a typical peptide bond would be stable for hundreds of years in water.

Life has evolved a handful of enzyme mechanisms that manage this catalysis. The research at issue here relied on two different ones. One is a zinc protease , where the positive charge of the zinc atom coordinates the peptide bond that’s being broken, key parts of the protease, and a water molecule. The protease partially pulls a proton off the water molecule, activating it to attack and break up the peptide bond.

The second protease the researchers use is called a cysteine protease . In this case, a cysteine (one of the amino acids) in the enzyme is activated to attack the peptide bond, creating a temporary intermediate where part of the protein being cut is chemically linked to the enzyme. A water molecule eventually breaks this intermediate apart, releasing the second part of the cut protein.

Both of these mechanisms require a handful of specific amino acids from the protease to be located in close proximity within the catalytic center of the protease. Other amino acids in the protease help ensure these key catalytic amino acids are brought together in the right place with the right orientation. The rest of the protease may also enforce a degree of specificity on what proteins get cut. Some proteases, like the ones active in our digestive system, can make cuts next to any amino acid. Others are slightly more selective, preferring to cut near positively or negatively charged amino acids. And a few are very highly specific, such as the protease that activates insulin, which only cuts near a very specific series of amino acids.

The people behind the new work, primarily from Nobel-winner David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, viewed designing a protease as a challenge. For one, the stability of the peptide bonds means that reactions wouldn’t take place without an effective catalyst. And to get that catalyst requires an extremely precise arrangement of specific amino acids. So it wasn’t obvious that the AI protein design tools the lab developed were up to the task.

Both projects took a similar approach. Just like evolution, they started with an existing protease. One was a zinc protease used in a crayfish’s digestive system. The other was a cysteine protease from yeast. In both cases, the protein structure was known, as were the key amino acids that catalyze cleaving other proteins. The design process started with these amino acids.

The design process started with software called RFdiffusion2, which creates a backbone for the enzyme (the backbone consists of the protein’s repeated peptide bonds). The researchers gave RFdiffusion2 a number of constraints. To start, any backbone it designed had to bring together the key catalytic amino acids needed for a functional protease. They also gave it a target amino acid sequence where the protease would eventually cut. The backbone had to accommodate that target sequence in close proximity to the catalytic center.

With a backbone laid out, the process next moved to ProteinMPNN, a tool that works along the backbone, populating it with specific amino acids. (That tool featured in Google’s efforts to watermark AI-designed proteins.) ProteinMPNN selects each amino acid based on a series of constraints. For starters, the amino acid must be compatible with the backbone folding up into its planned structure. Next, in critical areas, each amino acid chosen needs to be compatible with the formation of the enzyme’s catalytic site. And finally, in nearby areas, it has to be compatible with latching on to the intended target.

The researchers repeated this process dozens of times for both the cysteine and zinc proteases. For the cysteine protease, they made 12 different backbones and populated them with 69 different sets of amino acids. For the zinc project, they tried 135 different protein designs. They used AlphaFold3 to predict the structures of many of these designs and found nothing in the databases that looked much like them, confirming their tools weren’t simply stealing previously identified structures.

items.title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
items.summary: OpenAI engineer faces 5 years and $250K fine as FBI lobs foreign spy charges.
items.content:
It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships.

Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security.

To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day.

If convicted of violating laws against unlawful recordings, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, the FBI said.

OpenAI did not immediately move to eject Alfozan as a suspected spy. Instead, it gradually cut off his access to systems while working with the FBI to analyze the recording device’s contents. Once enough evidence was gathered, OpenAI timed Alfozan’s firing on Friday with the FBI’s arrest.

Citing a Trump memo ordering coordinated efforts to maintain America’s AI advantage, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated Alfozan’s arrest and vowed to continue policing efforts to spy on frontier labs like OpenAI.

It’s “essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said.

OpenAI hired Alfozan in July 2025, but the record suggests that he started acting suspiciously in the past few months.

In August, Alfozan allegedly used an OpenAI productivity agent to figure out where and when sensitive meetings were held, a recently unsealed affidavit submitted by FBI special agent Lydia Liang said.

Liang is a data analyst who joined the FBI after working for various tech companies. She analyzed the recording device that OpenAI found, which she said was a Chinese-made Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense.

According to Liang, the Seeed device “had been customized to obfuscate anything stored on the device, such as potentially intercepted audio communications.” And the microSD card had “a layout consistent with a potentially encrypted file system.”

In addition to reviewing Alfozan’s queries to OpenAI’s productivity agent, the FBI also reviewed an AI chatbot account associated with his spouse. Those logs showed user prompts referencing the Seeed device’s unique MAC address, the FBI said, while researching how to continuously record on that device, set up speech-triggered recording, and encrypt an SD card, among other queries.

“These written prompts attributable to Alfozan and/or his spouse, indicate that Alfozan inserted Recording Device 1 into the television in Conference Room 1 and was interested in building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing, among other things, a surreptitious audio listening and recording device,” Liang said.

CCTV footage allegedly caught Alfozan lurking outside the executive conference room on 10 different days in September alone, Liang noted.

Even more troubling to the FBI and OpenAI, it seemed that Alfozan had either deemed his plot successful and planned to plant another device or had noticed the camera stopped working and attempted to swap it out.

On the day he was seen checking behind the conference room TV, Alfozan also reported to OpenAI’s lost and found that he lost a bag. That bag had been left unattended in a printer room, the FBI said, where security personnel found it and discovered another Seeed device inside.

Alfozan seemingly did not suspect he had been caught, as he returned to the lost and found the next day and complained about missing items from the bag. When listing what had been taken, though, he did not mention the second recording device.

It remains unclear who the secret recordings were intended for, but that information may soon come out, as officials seem inclined to make an example of Alfozan at a time when maintaining AI dominance is a top Trump administration priority.

US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian said he would keep an eye on emerging threats in Silicon Valley.

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” Missakian said. “For us, it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

items.title: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
items.summary: Article URL: https://go.dev/blog/http-connection-reuse Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50090369 Points: 218 # Comments: 33
items.content:
Nicholas Husin and Damien Neil 14 October 2026

Take a look at the following function:

It sends a GET request to url and returns the HTTP status code.

Using HTTP/1 ( GODEBUG=http2client=0 ), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds.

That is almost 5 times faster! How is such a drastic performance difference possible?

To understand the difference, consider what happens on the network when we make an HTTP request.

Go’s net/http package supports HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2. All three run over TCP, and usually over TLS when talking to HTTPS endpoints. Making a request over a new connection looks something like this:

These round trips (plus some CPU time spent on TLS handshakes) add up quickly. In cross-region communications, one-way latencies often reach or exceed the 50 ms (100 ms RTT) shown in the diagram above. Compared to the 300 ms spent just setting up the connection, the HTTP request itself can be cheap to serve, taking only a little over 1 RTT when bandwidth is plentiful or the HTTP response is small.

Even in more favorable conditions, opening a new connection can still be expensive. Our opening benchmark queries index.golang.org , which is distributed worldwide and supports TLS 1.3. This means that latency is relatively low, and the TLS handshake can actually finish in just 1 RTT. Even so, the performance difference is still very noticeable.

To avoid paying this setup cost on every request, HTTP clients and servers try to reuse existing connections across multiple requests when possible. The mechanics of this differ based on the HTTP version:

In HTTP/1 (both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1), multiple requests and responses on the same connection are sent sequentially on the wire. If two GET requests are sent to index.golang.org over the same TCP connection, the responses arrive as a single stream of bytes:

As shown in the diagram, net/http.Get reads and parses the status line and headers from the byte stream to populate net/http.Response , then returns immediately. The response body remains unread on the connection and is consumed only as the caller reads from net/http.Response.Body .

Because responses are sent back-to-back on the same stream, net/http can only find the start of the next response after the current response body has been read to the very end (as determined by the Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding header).

Now look back at our example program, where we never read resp.Body :

Through Go 1.26, when resp.Body.Close is called, net/http sees that there is still an unread response body. Realizing that it cannot reuse the connection, it abandons the existing connection and creates new connections for its next requests, causing it to repeatedly incur the cost of establishing new connections.

(HTTP/2 does not have this problem. Because it multiplexes streams of frames over a single connection rather than sending responses strictly back-to-back, an unread response body on one stream does not block other requests from sharing the connection.)

This subtlety of HTTP/1 connection reuse can cause silent performance degradation in seemingly innocuous code.

As in our opening example, a client might only care about an API response’s status code. However, the API endpoint it is talking to might send bodies that provide more detailed but ultimately unused information, such as {"success": true, "message": "update processed"} . This will unfortunately cause connection reuse to fail.

Even programs that do read the response body can run into this issue if they stop just short of the end of the body. For example, encoding/json.Decoder stops reading as soon as it sees the closing } of a JSON object. If a server sends a JSON response terminated with a newline, decoding the JSON object will leave the newline still unread. The connection cannot be reused for a new request until that newline is consumed. Thus, a healthy connection might end up being abandoned, even though it was only a single byte away from being reusable.

The unread body problem has been a long-standing sharp edge. Over the years, many Go developers came up with their own workarounds. Most commonly, this is done by draining the response body prior to closing it:

While this works for small responses, if the unread body is large, establishing a new TCP connection can be faster than downloading and discarding the rest of the body. A better approach is to cap the number of bytes we are willing to drain:

However, a server might send a response body that trickles in slowly, so we also need to cap the time we spend draining:

Of course, we also do not want to block for up to 50 milliseconds when closing a response body. Instead, we can drain the body asynchronously in the background and let it race against subsequent requests:

As we can see, draining response bodies safely is surprisingly tricky and cumbersome. Worse, as the practice of draining response bodies spread, some nuances were often lost. This has led to misunderstandings such as attempting to drain response bodies for HTTP/2 connections, when doing so is unnecessary.

Starting in Go 1.27, net/http.Transport automatically does everything we have implemented in the code above: it will asynchronously drain an unread HTTP/1 response body for up to 50 ms or 256 KB. It also implements additional optimizations; for example, when a response contains the Connection: close header, draining the body is guaranteed to be wasted work, and it therefore skips doing so. Note that this behavior might evolve in future versions of Go, as other possible enhancements become apparent.

As a general best practice, we now recommend that users simply close their HTTP bodies once they no longer need them, like in our original example:

Go is all about simplicity. Let your code stay clean and simple, and let net/http deal with the complexities on your behalf.

items.title: Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/9/29/americans-social-activity-has-steeply-declined-in-the-past-30-years Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50089921 Points: 300 # Comments: 302
items.content:
In recent years, there has been extensive discussion of a social decline in the United States, including a U.S. surgeon general advisory in 2023 that declared American loneliness to be an “epidemic.”

Various surveys have tracked America’s social decline over the past few decades. Tracking data from the American Time Use Survey shows that Americans are spending more time alone and less time with friends than they were two decades ago. Perhaps most notably, the American Perspectives Survey has found that from 1990 to 2021, the percentage of Americans with five or more close friends dropped by 25 points , from 63% to 38%.

But while extensive public tracking data show general declines in Americans’ socialization, little, if any, public data show what this looks like for the average American — how the day-to-day activities Americans participate in have changed over the past few decades.

In a new survey , Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults and asked them how many times they engaged in various specific social activities in the past 12 months. These questions directly replicate the DDB Needham Life Style surveys, which tracked Americans’ participation in various activities from 1975-1999 and were referenced in Robert Putnam’s 2000 book “Bowling Alone.” In this analysis, Data for Progress’ 2026 data is compared with the DDB Needham Life Style survey from 1995, which is the earliest year in which full data for all comparison questions was available.

This survey finds significant, double-digit declines in Americans’ participation in key social activities from 1995 to 2026 .

The chart below compares the percentage of Americans who report participating in each tested activity at least one time in the past 12 months, between the 1995 and 2026 surveys. We find that Americans’ participation in various social activities has declined by double-digit margins, including attending a class or seminar (-22), entertaining people in your home (-21), attending church or a place of worship (-20), going on a picnic (-19), going to a club meeting (-19), playing cards (-19), going out to breakfast at a restaurant (-13), and doing volunteer work (-12).

A few activities have seen increased engagement: using the internet (+90), playing a home video game (+22), attending an exercise class (+14), going to a pop or rock concert (+13), and taking an airline trip for personal reasons (+5).

Methodology note: This analysis compares two surveys conducted using different methodologies, including differences in constructing sampling frames, modes, and weighting approaches. The findings below should be read as suggestive of trends, not a precise estimate of change. Please see the “Methodology” section below for more information.

One of the steepest declines in the survey is for “entertaining people in my home.” While in 1995, 88% of Americans reported entertaining others at home at least once in the past year, this number has declined to 67% in 2026.

Church attendance has dropped from 74% in 1995 to 54% in 2026.

The percentage of Americans who report having gone on a picnic in the past year has declined from 58% in 1995 to 39% in 2026.

There has also been a 19-point decline in attendance at club meetings, from 45% in 1995 to 26% in 2026.

This analysis adds to existing public data on America’s social decline. Previous reports have found that Americans are spending less time with others and reporting fewer close friends. This new analysis demonstrates that Americans are indeed spending less time in specific social settings, such as restaurants, churches, picnics, parties, bars, and social clubs.

The DDB Needham survey was conducted by Market Facts using a stratified quota sampling procedure that begins with a sampling frame acquired from commercial list brokers. The sample oversamples by demographics such as race, gender, and marital status to oversample lower propensity respondents. Finally, the survey contacted individuals via mail.

In comparison, the Data for Progress adult sample was conducted through web panel suppliers and ensured national representativeness via quota fielding and post-stratification weighting.

There is plenty of research on the compositional differences that exist across survey collection modes, and this is likely to affect these results as questions about religiosity and loneliness tend to demonstrate modal differences and social desirability biases. We understand that these factors are at play in our comparison, but find that the magnitude and consistency in trends across measures is a substantial signal about trends in behaviors nonetheless.

items.title: Passkeys are not a trap
items.summary: Article URL: https://scotthelme.co.uk/passkeys-are-not-a-trap/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50088935 Points: 539 # Comments: 697
items.content:
A post called Passkeys are a trap. Do not use them. has been doing the rounds over the last few days, making it pretty high on Hacker News, and I've had it sent to me many times with an 'is this true?' kind of vibe. It's written for "non-technical citizens of the web", and the headline advice is to stop using passkeys and go back to TOTP codes and passwords.

The post makes what appears to be one central claim: Passkeys support something called attestation, which lets a website ask for cryptographic proof of what made the passkey.

The author calls this a "hidden dial" and argues that sites will slowly turn it up, until you're only allowed to log in with approved software on an approved operating system, with no modifications, no LineageOS and no sharing your Netflix password. Throw in uBlock Origin, the FIDO Alliance membership list and the UK's image-scanning proposals, and the conclusion is that passkeys are "not designed to prioritize your interests". <that-escalated-quickly.gif>

It's a compelling story. It just doesn't match how any of this actually works...

The passkeys most people use are synced passkeys, stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden or whatever other software of your choosing. These passkeys don't give websites an attestation statement at all, and though a site can ask, what comes back is none . I know this because I wrote an opensource passkeys library and made it available to everyone.

If a consumer website decided tomorrow that it would only accept attested passkeys, it would lock out almost all of its own users, instantly. What website is going to do that? Besides, the guidance for consumer sites has been to not even request attestation for years now.

The post describes attestation as proving "that an approved passkey manager, operating system, and firmware are in use" which is simply not true.

When it is present, WebAuthn attestation tells the site the make and model of the authenticator, identified by its AAGUID , with a certificate chain from the vendor to back it up. It says nothing about your OS, your browser, your extensions, whether your phone is rooted or jailbroken, your firmware version, or even what colour it is.

This is the part that surprised me the most. For people who want stronger security, the post recommends a hardware security key like a YubiKey, because it "avoids OS-wide attestation".

YubiKeys are the authenticators that do attestation. Every one of them ships with a Yubico-issued attestation certificate, and enterprise attestation exists specifically so organisations can require approved hardware keys. I'd still recommend a YubiKey to anyone who wants one, they're excellent and I use them, but if attestation is the thing you're worried about, the post's own recommendation pushes you towards attestation rather than away from it!

The post holds up TOTP as "already" a great solution. TOTP is better than a password alone, absolutely, but it has one big weakness: you can type the code into the wrong website, just ask my good friend Troy Hunt . Phishing kits like Evilginx sit in the middle, relay your password and code to the real site in real time, and walk away with your session. This isn't theoretical, it's how a huge number of account takeovers happen today and we have the evidence to prove it.

This is the problem that passkeys solve. A passkey is bound to the domain it was created for, so your browser simply won't use your example.com passkey on examp1e.com . There's no code to read out and nothing for the user to get wrong. The author even concedes this in the addendum, saying that passkeys are domain-bound and resist man-in-the-middle attacks, but still tells readers to avoid them. Swapping a phishing-resistant credential for a phishable one is a really bad trade...

Keep using passkeys! Wherever a site offers one, take it, and store it in a password/passkey manager you trust. If you want to be able to move your credentials around, pick a provider that supports that. If you're worried about attestation creeping into consumer logins, then that's worth pushing back on, loudly (if it ever happens). But it hasn't happened, the biggest providers don't support it, and avoiding passkeys today while you wait for it won't protect you from anything, it just leaves you open to phishing.

I have some experience in this area:

I created WhyNoPasskeys.com to track the availability of passkeys on the Web.

I built and deployed passkeys support on my own SaaS company.

We built our own passkeys library and had it security reviewed.

I wrote about Security considerations when using Passkeys on your website .

I wrote Passkeys 101: An Introduction to Passkeys and How They Work .

I made our passkeys library opensource for everyone to use.

I've done extensive security testing of passkeys implementations.

I've openly acknowledged the limitations of not using attestation on passkeys.

I think most of all that it's important to say I use passkeys everywhere I can because they're currently the best thing we have available to protect our accounts. And they're not a trap.
